The question is, would a local market like what you have in mind be better? I think so.

There is less work itemizing and tracking things online, and people are able to eyeball and size up items more quickly.

Picture a giant secured warehouse, freely hosted on government owned land that people can just walk through, store, view, shop and trade items. Rather than giving each seller a glass "booth" behind lock and key (which would fail for so many reasons I won't get into) here is how I would do it.

Everything would just be stored out in the open. You would have to use a cheap solution for tags, and that would cost money. The tag identifies the a) item, b) the owner and c) its location in the warehouse (this is the hard problem that needs solving because things will get mixed up). RFID would work best because it does not run on battery. RFID location tracking would be essential for this to work.

Someone wanting that item would scan the tag and that would say they were interested. The owner of the item would be notified, and would be able to respond to all interested parties about what they wanted in return. The owner might even be able to scan a few items as an example, or take pictures of things not in the warehouse that are not in the market. Interested parties would respond by scanning their own item's tags and offering a trade. The original item owner would be able to browse all offers, and then make inquires "Do you have more?" "Do you have less?". The responding parties would be able to respond with modifications to the deal, going back and forth, until a deal was finalized. When a deal is finalized, both owners confirm the trade. The ownership of each item involved, is simply "switched" in the system. Bear in mind, under this system, one item cannot be split between two owners.

An item owner has the power at any time to move items out of the warehouse, decommissioning them from the market and taking them home.

Now.... involving the trading of services would have to be a bit different. They would be advertised in the "Services" section of the market, using tags the same way as products. However services would have to be backed by some force, so you can't just trade a service, never deliver, and then go run off with an item. Craigslist services works, I assume because two people are actually meeting and verifying the work is being performed. The marketplace has some flaws. In one scenario, a service provider performs an honest service, but the item owner says "he never did it." and screws the service provider. In the other scenario the service provider never delivers, while keeping the traded item. So we would have to devise a way so that services are performed in a trade, and then any products involved in the trade are then swapped to each respective owner, without ever leaving the warehouse.

I thought of a system of tokens and badges. I had an idea where a printed physical "token" could be traded by each party, which represents the completion of the service. Each person involved in the trade would also have their own identification badge. This helps to guarantee security and verification for each party - because with the use of a token, the two parties are physically meeting and verifying each others offerings (as if they were on Craigslist Services) while at the same time providing a way to verify back to the marketplace that the service has been performed. Once each party has traded their tokens, each party involved in the trade should be able to scan his/her token WITH his or her own identification badge. This tells the system,: "one guy has the other's token, so the Service must be completed."

Now I am sure there are many hacks to this system and that would cause a lot of economic damage, and there are also many risks like damage to the items. Would would be liable and who would pay?

Yes, it seems simpler just to have people meeting at a Farmer's market with a booth of items stored every week, but what are the chances you ever run into the magical person that has everything you need and vice versa. You might make relationships with people yes, but I only see that partnership lasting long if both of you are offering services.
